title: Fixed weights retained 80 percent efficiency in both states of 107 of 108 selected Allen models with independent noise
abstract: We tested one fixed positive readout across first and late 50 Hz response summaries in Allen cortical slice data. Each stored median was assigned as a model mean. Input noise was independent. A second-order cone method chose weights to maximize the smaller efficiency across states. Efficiency was squared signal-to-noise ratio divided by its state-specific optimum. Fixed weights retained at least 80 percent in both states in 107 of 108 selected input groups. First-state optimal weights fell below 80 percent in the late state in 18 groups. Median fixed-weight worst-state efficiency was 98.7 percent for mouse excitation, 98.6 percent for mouse inhibition and 95.4 percent for human excitation. A second optimizer agreed within 3.3e-8 efficiency units. Noise subtraction left only 25 groups, with three below 80 percent. Median-to-mean error, unknown covariance, separate input trials, different summary endpoints and selected slices prevent a neuronal decoding claim. Original code, aggregate evidence, hashes and a figure support reproduction. External records stay outside the bundle.

display.caption: One fixed positive readout across first and late response-summary states. Efficiency is relative to the ideal readout in each state. Independent noise and median-based model means are assumed. Source measurements: Allen Institute for Brain Science; Campagnola, Seeman and colleagues, Science 2022, doi:10.1126/science.abj5861.

citations.reason: Uses its first-state input grouping and model-mean convention. New code tests fixed weights across two states.
Prior covariance-cap model in one response state; the present model tests state transfer under independence.
Prior shared-gain test on response amplitudes. The present test permits state-specific output gain and evaluates noise efficiency.
Established cone programming and bisection methods.
